title: Can Mold Grow in Air Ducts?
h1: Can Mold Grow Inside Air Ducts?
description: Mold can grow in air ducts when moisture, dust and darkness come together. Here are the signs, the common causes in local homes and what to do next.
quick_answer: Yes, mold can grow inside air ducts when moisture gets in and sits on dust and debris. Common causes are condensation on poorly insulated ducts, leaks near the indoor coil, clogged drain lines and high indoor humidity. A musty smell when the system runs or visible growth around registers are the usual warning signs.
body:
Mold needs three things: moisture, something to feed on and a place where it won't be disturbed. Air ducts can offer all three. Dust and debris provide food, the inside of a duct is dark, and moisture can come from several sources tied to your HVAC system or your home.

How does moisture get into ducts?

Condensation

When cold air runs through a duct in a warm, humid space, the outside of the duct can sweat if the insulation is thin, torn or compressed. Moisture can also form inside ducts and at registers when cold supply air meets humid indoor air. Coastal homes with higher humidity see this more often.

Problems at the indoor coil and drain pan

The indoor coil pulls water out of the air every time the AC runs. That water is supposed to drain away. If the drain pan is cracked, rusted or sloped wrong, or the condensate line is clogged, water can sit near the coil and the start of the duct system, where mold grows easily.

Leaks and outside air

Roof leaks over an attic duct, plumbing leaks near a hall closet unit, or disconnected ducts pulling damp air from a crawl space can all bring moisture into the system.

An oversized system

An AC that's too large for the home cools quickly and shuts off before it removes enough humidity. The home can stay damp even though the temperature looks fine, which encourages mold in the ducts and around the house.

What are the signs of mold in your ducts?

  • A musty, earthy smell that gets stronger when the system turns on.
  • Dark spots or fuzzy growth on register covers, return grilles or the inside of the duct opening.
  • Growth or water staining around the indoor unit or drain pan.
  • Allergy-like symptoms that ease when you're away from home.
  • Condensation or water drips at ceiling registers.

Not every dark spot at a register is mold. Dust and soot can look similar, especially around supply registers where air passes over the ceiling. A closer inspection, and testing when needed, sorts that out.

Is mold in ducts dangerous?

Mold spores can bother people with allergies, asthma or sensitive airways, and a moldy duct system can spread spores through the whole house every time it runs. If anyone in the home is having health symptoms, talk with a doctor. On our end, the goal is to find and fix the moisture source and clean the affected parts of the system.

What should you do if you suspect mold?

  1. Don't scrape or vacuum it yourself. Disturbing it can spread spores through the house.
  2. Check the filter. Replace it if it's dirty or damp.
  3. Look around the indoor unit for standing water, rust or a wet drain pan.
  4. Have the system inspected. A technician can look at the coil, drain, insulation and ducts, often with a camera.

How is mold in ducts fixed?

Fixing it starts with the moisture. Cleaning without solving the cause just means the mold comes back. Depending on what we find, the work may include:

  • Clearing the condensate drain and repairing or replacing the drain pan.
  • Repairing torn or thin duct insulation to stop condensation.
  • Sealing disconnected or leaking ducts.
  • Cleaning and sanitizing the affected ducts and registers.
  • Cleaning the indoor coil and blower.
  • Replacing duct sections that are too far gone, especially flexible ducts with mold in the liner.

Our air duct cleaning and sanitizing service covers the cleaning and duct repair side. For humidity and ongoing prevention, see our indoor air quality options.

How can you keep mold out of your ducts?

  • Change filters on schedule.
  • Have the coil, drain pan and condensate line checked during yearly maintenance.
  • Keep indoor humidity in a moderate range, using a dehumidifier if your home runs damp.
  • Fix roof and plumbing leaks near ducts quickly.
  • Make sure attic ducts are properly insulated and sealed.

If you've already had mold cleaned out of the system once, pay close attention to the drain line and humidity afterward. Those are the two things most likely to bring it back, and they're both easy to check during a routine tune-up.
faqs: What does mold in air ducts smell like?
Most people describe it as musty, earthy or like a damp closet or wet towel. The smell is usually strongest right after the system turns on.
Can I clean mold out of air ducts myself?
It is not recommended. Disturbing mold can spread spores through the house, and the moisture source still needs to be found and fixed. A professional inspection and cleaning is the safer route.
Will mold come back after duct cleaning?
It can if the moisture problem is not fixed. Clearing drains, repairing insulation, sealing leaks and controlling humidity are what keep it from returning.
Do flexible ducts need to be replaced if they have mold?
Often, yes. The inner liner of flex duct is hard to clean thoroughly once mold has grown into it, so replacing the affected sections is usually the better fix.
Does UV Light Kill Mold in Air Ducts?

UV-C light can kill mold, but only on surfaces it shines on directly and long enough. In an HVAC system, that's mainly the evaporator coil and drain pan near the lamp. It can't reach most of the ductwork, and it won't remove mold that's already growing or fix the moisture problem behind it. Mold in ducts usually needs cleaning plus a moisture fix.
Can Air Duct Cleaning Remove Mold Spores?

Professional duct cleaning can remove mold growth and much of the spore-laden dust from metal ducts, registers and the blower area. It will not keep mold away unless the moisture problem behind it is fixed, and badly affected flexible duct usually needs to be replaced rather than cleaned.
